J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges: "If a symmetric polynomial's leading monomial has exponents a_i > a_j with i<j, then exchanging those exponents produces a monomial that is larger in the degree reverse lexicographic order." First-choice line 29 is exactly that conditional: the monomial displayed at line 27 (the exponents of LM p with positions i and j swapped) "must also appear in $p$, and if $a_i > a_j$ then it would be larger than $\map {LM} p$, a contradiction." Under the source's active assumptions -- line 5 (< is the degree reverse lexicographic order), line 7 (LM f is the unique <-largest monomial appearing in f), line 1 (p symmetric), line 20 (LM p = x_1^{a_1} ... x_n^{a_n}) and the standing assumption of line 24 (a_i > a_j for some 1 <= i < j <= n) -- line 29 asserts precisely the 'would be larger' claim the response denies. So J1 = YES.

J2_evidence_specified.justification: A complete concrete instance is given: "In K[x1,x2] with the degree reverse lexicographic order, the symmetric polynomial p = x1^2 x2 + x1 x2^2 has leading monomial x1^2 x2, but swapping the exponents gives x1 x2^2, which is smaller, not larger." Ring, variables, order, polynomial, its leading monomial, the index pair (implicitly i=1, j=2) and the swapped monomial are all named; nothing is left for the reader to supply.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Exact check of exactly the supplied witness, script kept. Encoding the standard degree reverse lexicographic order (equal total degree, rightmost nonzero entry of a-b negative means a > b): p = x1^2 x2 + x1 x2^2 is symmetric (the transposition x1<->x2 exchanges its two monomials), its monomial exponent vectors are (2,1) and (1,2), and cmp gives (2,1) > (1,2), so LM p = x1^2 x2 as the response says, with (a_1,a_2) = (2,1). The hypothesis of line 24 holds with i=1 < j=2 since a_1 = 2 > a_2 = 1. The line-27 monomial is then x_1^{a_2} x_2^{a_1} = x1 x2^2; the script confirms it does appear in p (so the first half of line 29 holds) and that it compares SMALLER than LM p, not larger. Line 29's assertion therefore fails on an instance satisfying all of the source's active assumptions, which is a genuine refutation of line 29 as written. The script also checks that the convention used is the one under which the source's own line 22 (a_1 >= ... >= a_n) is true -- for every symmetric orbit tested in 2 and 3 variables the <-largest arrangement is the nonincreasing one -- so the witness does not smuggle in the opposite orientation of the order to manufacture the failure. I did not attempt a Lean check: faithfully formalizing degrevlex leading monomials was out of proportion to the 20-minute budget, and the arithmetic here is a finite comparison.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The consequence the response draws is confined to the sub-argument: "the claim that if there exists a_i > a_j with i<j then swapping yields a larger monomial is false; it yields a smaller monomial", i.e. "lines 0024-0029 contain a false assertion". It explicitly declines to extend this to the statement being justified -- it had concluded "line 0020-0022 might be true" and, separately, that line 11 "is actually correct" -- and it never claims the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Polynomials or the overall decomposition fails. That is the correct scope: only the justification at line 29 is broken, and my check agrees line 22 is true under this order. No overreach.

notes: Convention dependency a second reader should weigh: the witness refutes line 29 under the standard degrevlex definition (rightmost nonzero entry of a-b negative => a greater). Under the mirrored convention the <-largest arrangement would be the nondecreasing one; then this p would have LM = x1 x2^2, the line-24 hypothesis a_1 > a_2 would not hold for it and the witness would not apply -- but in that case the source's line 22 would itself be false. Either way one of lines 22 / 29 is false; the response picked 29 and its witness is exact under the standard convention that makes line 22 true. Also worth noting for adjudication: the source's proof structure at line 24 assumes a_i > a_j (i < j) to derive a contradiction, which if sound would give a nondecreasing exponent sequence, the opposite of line 22 -- a second reader may see the defect as a flipped inequality; the response's witness targets the same spot. The response's second candidate (line 17, sigma_1..sigma_k instead of sigma_1..sigma_n) is not the first choice and I did not grade it.
